lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Owned the weekly carrier scorecards for the regional managers and the monthly review meeting that discussed them.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites by redesigning slotting rules with the floor supervisors and retraining 45 pickers on the new layout.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: Experience is not newest-first: the 2018–2023 Crestline role appears above the 2024 Harbor Payments internship.
items.because: The ordering obscures the more recent product work and makes the chronology harder to follow.

items.says: The ongoing Product Lead work does not lead the page.
items.because: Leading with it would establish the product contribution before its academic context.

items.says: The move from the product internship and MBA to Diesel Mechanic is dated but unexplained.
“Under 5 days per job” gives no reference point for judging the dry-dock duration.
“Maintained hydraulic winch systems” does not identify the maintenance performed.
The inspection reference gives the reason for the records but no inspection or operational outcome.
The monthly review meeting does not say what the scorecard reviews changed.
items.because: A hiring manager cannot tell whether the reviews led to a carrier decision or improved performance.

items.says: “Weekly carrier scorecards” does not identify the carrier performance they assessed.
“Owned the weekly carrier scorecards” frames the work as an assigned duty rather than an action taken.
“The monthly review meeting that discussed them” refers back to the scorecards roundaboutly.
The reduction in forecast error is buried at the end instead of leading the Crestline entry.
items.because: The measured result is easier to miss and would make a stronger first impression.

items.says: The driver-hours saving is buried, and “which saved” leaves its cause ambiguous.
items.because: A reader may miss the saving or credit the telematics contract rather than the route-planning rollout.

items.says: The route-planning rollout does not say what changed in route planning.
The comparison with the three-step flow adds detail the line does not need unless the old flow’s step count matters.
Scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close defines RICE Reach incorrectly.
items.because: Reach measures tickets a feature would address, while predicted closures also reflect effectiveness and could be counted again in Impact.

items.says: The Reach-scoring clause adds process detail that slows the line.
items.because: It takes space before the reader learns what the prioritization produced.

items.says: “Prioritized the dispute roadmap” does not identify the initiative selected or decision made.
items.because: The choice is more informative than the framework alone.

items.says: The next quarter’s roadmap priority is buried after the methods and is not named.
items.because: A reader may miss the decision and cannot judge the significance of the interviews and business case.

items.says: “Sizing the loss by segment” names an analysis without giving its finding.
Session randomization does not support reporting the lift as an effect on distinct merchants’ customers.
items.because: A customer can have multiple sessions in different variants, so the difference is a session-level result without separate customer-level analysis.

items.says: The checkout A/B test and five-point lift repeat a test and result already reported in this entry.
items.because: The earlier bullet gives the conversion figures and test scale, so repetition uses space without adding another result.

items.says: “A follow-up roadmap” does not identify the proposal leadership funded.
“Launched a surplus-food pickup app” does not identify the product or launch decision personally owned.
items.because: The redistribution figure shows the venture’s result, not the Product Lead contribution.

items.says: “To 3,100 students with two dining halls” leaves the dining halls’ role unclear.
“Food that would have been thrown away” is wordier than necessary.
The increase from 400 to 1,150 weekly active users is incorrectly stated as 150%.
items.because: The gain of 750 divided by 400 is 187.5%.

items.says: “Pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews” obscures what the interviews informed.
The rise from 75% to 95% is incorrectly called a 20% increase.
items.because: It is a 20-percentage-point rise, or approximately 26.7% relative to the starting rate.

items.says: “Based on the model” does not identify the main source of the estimated saving.
The client’s pilot-funding decision is left behind the sizing work.
The $2.4M annual saving has no comparison with current scheduling costs.
items.because: A reader cannot tell the estimate’s scale relative to the costs it would reduce.

items.says: Adoption by front-desk staff is stated without saying what improved.
The passive wording about mapping intake and shortening the form hides the candidate’s actions.
The adoption result is buried in a trailing clause.
“The intake form was shortened” does not show what was removed or simplified.
“The final recommendation” does not say which scheduling change leaders approved testing.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what the pilot would change.

items.says: The approval of the scheduling pilot is left at the end of the bullet.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the client decision only after the presentation detail.

items.says: The pilot approval repeats the pilot decision already reported in the practicum entry.
items.because: Funding and approval appear to describe the same decision without establishing separate outcomes.
